entries.proof: ScopeRef's constructor is private and every `new ScopeRef(...)` in the module sits inside one of its own static factories, so kind and the optional ids are always assigned together, at four sites and nowhere else. The only site that yields kind "project" is ScopeRef.project(tenantId, projectId), whose projectId parameter is a required ProjectId; no factory can build a project scope with an absent projectId, and decodeScopeRef reaches the class only through those same factories. Control arrives at this guard only after the kind "tenant" branch has returned, so the scope here is a project scope and scope.projectId === undefined is constantly false. Replacing the test with false therefore selects the identical branch on every input. The complementary mutant that replaces it with true, which would throw for every project scope, is killed — the outward signature of an unreachable guard.

entries.mutated: { throw new TypeError("Project scope requires a Project ID"); }
entries.proof: This block is the throw guarded by scope.projectId === undefined, and that condition is constantly false for the reason recorded against the condition itself: kind "project" is reachable only through ScopeRef.project, which requires a ProjectId. A block that never executes contributes no value, no exception, and no effect to any observation, so emptying it cannot change what any caller sees. Stryker reports this mutant as NoCoverage rather than Survived because no test executes it, which is a consequence of the unreachability rather than a coverage gap some future test could close.

The mutated literal is the message argument of a TypeError constructed only inside the unreachable project-id guard. Because that guard's condition is constantly false, the TypeError is never constructed and the literal is never read, so replacing it with the empty string changes no value any caller, log, or assertion can observe. This is a strictly stronger claim than the message-text tolerance the classifier grants reachable throw sites: the string is not merely unasserted, it is never materialized, and a test that pinned it would be asserting on a value the program cannot produce.

ScopeKind is a closed union of three members, and control reaches this guard only after the tenant and project branches have returned, so scope.kind is "workspace" here. The only factory that produces a workspace scope is ScopeRef.workspace, whose implementation passes either requireWorkspace(projectOrWorkspace) — which returns a WorkspaceId or throws — or the workspace argument on the branch where it has already been tested as defined. Neither path can store an absent workspaceId, so the condition is constantly false and replacing it with false selects the same branch on every input. The complementary mutant replacing it with true, which would reject every workspace scope, is killed.

entries.mutated: { throw new TypeError("Workspace scope requires a Workspace ID"); }
entries.proof: The guarded block throws for a workspace scope carrying no workspace id, a state ScopeRef.workspace cannot construct: both of its paths resolve the id through requireWorkspace or through the workspace argument on the branch where it is already known to be defined. The block is therefore unreachable, and emptying an unreachable block cannot change any observable behavior. Stryker reports it as NoCoverage because no test executes it, which is the expected signature of unreachability rather than a missing test.

This literal is the message of a TypeError constructed only inside the unreachable workspace-id guard in encodeScopeRef, so it is never materialized and emptying it is unobservable. The identical literal also appears in requireWorkspace, where it is reachable and its own mutant is killed by the tests that drive ScopeRef.workspace with a non-workspace id. The entry is anchored to the enclosing symbol precisely so this proof cannot be read as covering that other site: the two literals are the same text and different facts.

kind is a function of which optional ids a ScopeRef holds. The private constructor is reached only from the three factories, which produce "tenant" with neither id, "project" with a projectId and no workspaceId, and "workspace" with a workspaceId, so the pair (projectId defined, workspaceId defined) determines kind uniquely: (false, false) is tenant, (true, false) is project, and anything holding a workspaceId is workspace. optionalIdEquals returns true only when its two operands agree on definedness, so the two conjuncts that follow this one force both receivers into the same row of that table and hence to the same kind. The kind comparison is therefore implied by the conjuncts after it, and replacing it with true cannot change the value of the chain. Nor can it change anything else: the conjuncts the original short-circuited away are TextId.equals calls, which are total and pure and return false rather than throwing for a mismatched id type. The mutants replacing this test with false, and the equality operator with !==, are both killed.

The only effect of this statement is the assignment remaining[dimension] = left, and current was read from remaining[dimension] on the line immediately above. Original and mutant therefore differ on exactly one class of input: current !== undefined && left === current. There the original skips the assignment and leaves remaining[dimension] holding current, while the mutant performs it and writes left. Because left === current on precisely that branch, and remaining holds primitive numbers with no reference or identity semantics to leak a difference, both leave the same key holding the same value. Assigning a key that already exists also leaves insertion order untouched, and current !== undefined guarantees the key exists on exactly that branch. Order could not matter regardless: ResourceCeiling's constructor iterates the fixed RESOURCE_DIMENSIONS list rather than Object.keys, so neither the Object.keys(remaining).length test in narrowResources nor the ceiling it constructs can vary with it. On every other input the two conditions agree and the same assignment happens or is skipped in both. The claim therefore holds through the whole call chain, not merely inside narrow, and no test written against the resulting ceiling could distinguish the two.

The mutant leaves `limit > allowance` as the sole test, so it differs from the original only where allowance is undefined, and there the original is false by short-circuit while the mutant evaluates `limit > undefined`. JavaScript's abstract relational comparison takes the string path only when both operands are strings; undefined never is, so both operands go through ToNumber, undefined becomes NaN, and every comparison against NaN is false. The mutant is therefore false wherever the original short-circuited, and identical everywhere else because the conjunct it dropped was already true. No input can separate them: allowance is a plain local read of parentRemainder.limit(dimension) taken before the comparison, so the dropped conjunct guarded no side effect and no throw, and limit arrives from ResourceCeiling's own entries, where the constructor has already established it is a non-negative safe integer. Even a caller passing a hostile subclass whose entries yield a non-number cannot help, because the NaN result holds for every value undefined can be compared against. The complementary mutant replacing this test with false, which would report no child as widening, is killed.

This guard exists for the type checker rather than for the program. RunInit declares `parent?: RunId` and the package compiles with exactOptionalPropertyTypes, so writing `parent: this.parent` — an expression of type RunId | undefined — is rejected at this very call site; the conditional spread is the standard way the codebase satisfies that rule. Forcing the test false spreads the key unconditionally, so where the original omitted `parent` the mutant supplies it holding undefined. The literal is an argument to `new Run(...)` and reaches nothing else: Run's constructor assigns `this.parent = init.parent`, never asks whether the key is present, never enumerates init, and never spreads it onward, so a missing key and a key holding undefined are the same read. Everything downstream reads the field, not the literal — toData emits `this.parent?.value ?? null`. The sibling spreads in Turn.fromData are killed instead of surviving precisely because their else branch constructs an id from the absent value and throws; this one only repeats a value already in hand.

RunInit declares `terminal?: TerminalSnapshot`, and under exactOptionalPropertyTypes a TerminalSnapshot | undefined cannot be assigned to it, so this spread is guarded to keep the key out of the literal rather than to keep undefined out of the Run. With the test forced false the key is always written, carrying whatever the parameter holds. Run's constructor consumes the literal by name three times over — it assigns this.terminal from init.terminal, it selects the lifecycle by testing `init.terminal === undefined`, and it compares the snapshot's Run against this.id — and every one of those is a value read that sees undefined whether the key was omitted or written as undefined. No caller counts the literal's keys, tests `in`, or forwards it; the literal is constructed and consumed in one expression. So the two spellings build the same Run, with the same lifecycle kind and the same absent terminal snapshot, and no observation of the returned Run can separate them.

The local this guards was already resolved on the lines above, where `object["cacheLineage"] === null` decides between undefined and a decoded lineage, so the else branch here names a bound variable and constructs nothing. Forcing the test false writes the key unconditionally, holding the same undefined the original omitted. TurnInit declares `cacheLineage?: TurnCacheLineage` and exactOptionalPropertyTypes is what forbids the unconditional spelling in the source, which is the only reason the conditional is written at all. Turn's constructor reads init.cacheLineage by name and branches on it being undefined to decide whether to freeze a copy, so both spellings leave this.cacheLineage undefined and the Turn identical. The two neighbouring spreads for checkpoint and result are killed rather than equivalent because their else branches pass an absent string to new RunCheckpointId and new ContentRef, which throw; the contrast is what makes this site's survival a property of the value rather than a gap in the decode tests.

The guarded value is the local `changes.checkpoint ?? this.checkpoint` computed at the top of transition, so the else branch republishes a variable and evaluates no constructor. Under exactOptionalPropertyTypes a RunCheckpointId | undefined cannot be assigned to TurnInit's `checkpoint?: RunCheckpointId`, which is why the spread is conditional in the first place; the mutant writes the key unconditionally and it holds undefined exactly where the original left it out. Turn's constructor assigns this.checkpoint = init.checkpoint and then tests `this.checkpoint === undefined` for the rule that a suspended Turn carries one, and both are reads of the value rather than of the key set. Since the literal is consumed by that constructor alone and never enumerated, spread onward, or probed with `in`, every Turn either spelling can produce is identical, including the throw the suspended rule raises.

This spread carries the local `changes.result ?? this.result`, already computed, so making its test constantly false writes a key holding undefined where the original wrote no key, and evaluates nothing new. TurnInit declares `result?: ContentRef`; exactOptionalPropertyTypes rejects assigning ContentRef | undefined to it, which is the sole reason the assignment is guarded rather than written plainly. The constructor assigns this.result = init.result and separately tests `this.result === undefined` to refuse a succeeded or failed Turn without one, so a Turn built either way holds the same field and raises the same refusal on the same inputs. Nothing in the package inspects the init literal's key set: it is built and passed to new Turn in a single expression and is unreachable afterwards, so no observation of the resulting Turn, its encoding, or the errors it raises can separate the two.

Unlike its two neighbours this spread carries the receiver's own field straight through a transition, so with the test forced false the literal always names cacheLineage and holds whatever this.cacheLineage held, undefined included. The conditional is present because TurnInit declares `cacheLineage?: TurnCacheLineage` and exactOptionalPropertyTypes forbids assigning the optional field to the optional parameter directly. Turn's constructor reads init.cacheLineage and branches on it being undefined, freezing a copy of turn and promptPrefix when it is present and storing undefined when it is not, so the field the new Turn ends up with is the same under either spelling and its encoding, which writes null for an absent lineage, is byte-identical. The literal never escapes the call, is never enumerated and is never tested with `in`, so no test of the transition's result can tell the key apart from its absence.

Forcing this conjunct true leaves `if (isTerminal(this.status)) return this`, so original and mutant differ only for a Turn that is terminal and still holds a lease. No such Turn exists. The constructor refuses one outright — `(this.status.kind === "suspended" || isTerminal(this.status)) && this.lease.holder !== undefined` throws "Suspended and terminal Turns must be unheld" — and it is the single gate into the class: TurnCodec decodes through Turn.fromData, which calls the constructor, and every transition rebuilds through new Turn as well. The two predicates are the same isTerminal call against the same status field, so the state the mutated conjunct exists to exclude is exactly the state the constructor has already made unconstructible. On every reachable Turn the conjunct is therefore constantly true and the branch selected is identical, with or without it.

Dropping this disjunct leaves the refusal resting on the lease alone, and the lease already refuses every Turn the status test would have caught. The constructor pins holder to status: a queued Turn requires an unheld epoch-zero lease, a suspended or terminal Turn must be unheld, and only a running Turn may hold one. ExactTurnLease.admits requires `this.holder !== undefined` before it can return true, so for any Turn whose status is not running admits is false, !admits is true, and the same lease.invalid error is raised with the same message. For a running Turn the disjunct is false and contributes nothing. The extra evaluation the mutant performs is harmless: admits reads frozen fields and calls instanceof, TextId.equals and PrincipalRef.equals, all total and pure, and it cannot reach now.getTime() because that conjunct sits behind the holder test that no non-running Turn passes.

This conjunct is the type narrowing that lets the next line compare expiresAtTime against now.getTime(); its runtime effect is subsumed twice over. Control reaches it only after `this.holder !== undefined` has passed, and TurnLease's protected constructor throws "Held Turn leases require an expiration" for a held lease with no expiry, so a lease that gets this far always has one and the conjunct is constantly true. Even if it did not, the mutant would compute `undefined > now.getTime()`, and JavaScript's relational comparison sends undefined through ToNumber to NaN, which compares false against every value — the same answer the short circuit gave. The comparison the mutant additionally evaluates is pure, and now.getTime() is unreachable behind the holder test anyway, so nothing observable changes.

The disjunct is implied by the one before it. admits returns true only when `expiresAtTime !== undefined && expiresAtTime > now.getTime()` holds, and currentExpiresAtTime was read from the very same private field on the line above; the field is set once in the constructor and the instance is frozen, so nothing can change it between the two reads. When admits succeeds the field is defined and the disjunct is false; when admits fails the first disjunct has already selected the throw. Removing it therefore selects the same branch on every input. It is written because the later comparison `expiresAt.getTime() <= currentExpiresAtTime` needs the narrowing that admits, being a plain boolean method, cannot give the checker, and it evaluates nothing and raises nothing of its own.

Reaching this disjunct means `this.holder === undefined` was false, so the lease is held, and TurnLease's constructor admits no held lease without an expiration — it throws "Held Turn leases require an expiration" before such an instance can exist, and every construction path in the file, including restore, unclaimed, fence, claim, renew and the decoder, goes through it. So on every reachable lease this disjunct is constantly false and the branch is decided by the two around it. The mutant does evaluate `expiresAtTime > now.getTime()` where the original short-circuited, but that state is unreachable, and reclaim has already called ensureFutureExpiration(expiresAt, now), which reads now.getTime() on every call, so even the evaluation would add nothing observable.

Forcing this true leaves `holder === null || isPrincipalRefData(holder)`, and isPrincipalRefData answers false for undefined on its own: its first line rejects anything whose typeof is not "object", and typeof undefined is "undefined". So the mutant returns the same false the short circuit produced. The conjunct is present for the checker, because noUncheckedIndexedAccess types object["holder"] as JsonValue | undefined while isPrincipalRefData takes JsonValue. It is doubly redundant at runtime: hasExactJsonKeys has already established the payload carries exactly the four named keys before this conjunct is reached, and a value decoded from JSON is never undefined regardless. Nothing here can throw or record anything, so no input distinguishes the two.

Number.isSafeInteger, the conjunct immediately after this one, performs no coercion: it returns false for every argument that is not a number, so a string, boolean, null, array or object epoch is rejected by it whether or not the typeof test ran first. The mutant therefore computes the same boolean on every payload, and both spellings send a malformed epoch down the same codec.invalid path with the same message. The typeof test earns its place only in the type system, where it narrows JsonValue | undefined to number so that `epoch >= 0` on the following line is accepted — Number.isSafeInteger is declared as returning boolean rather than as a type predicate, so it cannot do that narrowing itself. Neither operand has a side effect, so nothing else can separate them.

This disjunct is subsumed by `!Number.isSafeInteger(epoch)` two lines below it, which is true for every value that is not a number because Number.isSafeInteger coerces nothing. Any epoch the removed test would have rejected is rejected by the surviving one, and the codec.invalid error raised carries the same `${name} is malformed` text either way, so a caller sees an identical failure. Where epoch is a number the disjunct is false and contributes nothing. It is written for the narrowing: under strict typing epoch is JsonValue | undefined, and both `epoch < 0` and the epoch field of the frozen token that is returned require it to be a number, which a boolean-returning helper cannot establish. The mutant's extra evaluations are pure.

This conjunct guards the else arm, where left is known to be a ContentRef, and forcing it true leaves `left.equals(right)`. The two spellings can differ only when right is undefined, and there TextId.equals — which ContentRef inherits and does not override — answers false rather than throwing: its first test is `typeof other === "object"`, and typeof undefined is "undefined", so it returns before touching a private field. The original returns false by short circuit and the mutant returns the same false from the call, on every pair of arguments. Both operands are already-bound locals, equals is pure and total, and the function's only caller compares a commit's tree checkpoint with a checkpoint's tree inside a boolean chain, so there is nothing else for a difference to leak through. The mutants replacing the same test with its negation, and the whole conjunction with true or false, are all killed by the four tree pairings.

The conjunct before this one has already established that the commit's kind is "checkpoint" or "result", and RunCommit's validateClosedShape refuses either of those without a turn writer: neither kind is handled by the root, merge, invocation, eventDelivery, undo or migration branches, so both fall through to the final block, which throws "Turn-authored commit fields are invalid" unless writer.kind is "turn". That check runs on construction, and RunCommitCodec decodes through RunCommit.fromData, which builds through the same constructor, so every commit listCommits can yield satisfies it. The conjunct is therefore constantly true wherever it is evaluated, and it is written because the three token comparisons after it read commit.writer.token, which the checker only permits once the writer union has been narrowed. The mutant replacing the same comparison with !== is killed, as is the string mutant emptying "turn".

By the time this disjunct is evaluated the Turn has already been held to the token: the second statement of the method calls turn.requireToken(token, now), which throws a lease.invalid AgentCoreError unless the status is running and the lease admits the token. The local is a frozen record read once, and nothing between the two points can change it, so the status is "running" here on every path that reaches the disjunct and it is constantly false. Removing it therefore selects the same branch always. It reads as the join restating one of its own preconditions rather than as an untested rule, and the complementary mutant that forces it true — which would refuse every scope — is killed by the tests that load a scope successfully.

checkpointCommit is bound by a conditional whose else arm is requireStored(this.loadCommit(tx, checkpoint.commit), ...), and requireStored throws a turn.invalid-state error rather than returning undefined. Its then arm yields undefined only when checkpoint is undefined, and this disjunct sits inside `checkpoint !== undefined && (...)`, so control cannot arrive here with the then arm's value. The variable is therefore always a RunCommit at this point and the test is constantly false. It is written to narrow RunCommit | undefined for the six clauses after it that read checkpointCommit's fields directly. The missing-record test proves the throw it is standing in for is the one that actually fires: deleting the checkpoint commit row is refused by requireStored with its own message, never by the scope mismatch this disjunct would raise.

The optional call can only differ from a plain one if subjectTurn is undefined here, and it cannot be. Two clauses earlier the chain short-circuits unless checkpointCommit.kind is "checkpoint", and a commit of that kind reaches validateClosedShape's final block, which throws unless subjectTurn is defined; RunCommitCodec decodes through RunCommit.fromData and so through that constructor, so no stored commit escapes it. Reaching this clause therefore means subjectTurn is a TurnId and both spellings call TurnId.equals with the same receiver and argument. The chain is written because the declared type stays TurnId | undefined for the whole class, not because this site can see an absent one. A test could only tell the two apart by producing a checkpoint commit without a subject Turn, which the record's own constructor makes unconstructible.

Control reaches this clause only after the kind, Run, branch, subject Turn and pins clauses have all been false, and the kind clause being false means the commit's kind is "checkpoint". validateClosedShape sends that kind to its final block, which throws "Turn-authored commit fields are invalid" unless content is defined, and every stored commit passes through it because the codec decodes through the constructor. So content is a ContentRef whenever this expression is evaluated, the optional call and the plain call invoke the same ContentRef.equals, and the guard against undefined is a type-level obligation rather than a runtime possibility. The tree-checkpoint comparison one line below is the genuinely optional one, and its mutants are killed by the four pairings; this one names a field the commit's shape rules require.

The index cannot be out of range. The disjunct before this one returns early unless edges.length equals commit.parents.length, and ordinal is the callback index supplied by edges.some, so it runs from zero to edges.length - 1 and every position it names exists in parents. RunCommit's constructor builds parents with Object.freeze([...init.parents]), a dense copy of a spread, so no position inside that range holds a hole either. The optional chain is written because noUncheckedIndexedAccess types an element access as possibly undefined; at runtime it never short-circuits, and both spellings read the same RunCommitId's value. The tests that prune a parent edge, tamper with its value, and shift its ordinal all exercise this comparison and pin the error it raises.

entries.mutated: { throw invalidRun("Acceptance criteria must declare unique identities"); }
entries.proof: This block is the throw guarded by reserved.registry === registry, and that comparison is constantly false: the loop refuses a repeated criterion id at the store check above it, before the reserve, and distinct ids always give RunAdmissionRegistry.reserve a key it has not seen, which makes it return a new registry rather than the receiver. A block that never executes contributes no exception, no value and no effect to any observation, so emptying it changes nothing a caller, a stored record or an assertion can see. The registry the loop goes on to build is assembled from reserved.registry either way.

The literal is the message of an AgentCoreError constructed only inside the unreachable duplicate-identity guard in the genesis loop, and it is never constructed: the store check one line above refuses a repeated criterion id first, so the reserve always returns a changed registry and the throw never runs. Replacing the text with the empty string therefore changes no value any caller, log or assertion can read, which is a stronger claim than the message-text tolerance granted to reachable throw sites — the string is not merely unasserted, the program cannot produce it.

The disjunct above this loop body already refuses a repeated identity. Each iteration first tests loadAcceptanceCriterion(tx, criterion.id) !== undefined and throws "Run genesis identifiers already exist", and the loop inserts each criterion before moving to the next, so the second declaration of an id is refused there and never reaches the reserve. Criteria whose ids differ produce different acceptance obligation keys, and RunAdmissionRegistry.reserve returns a new registry whenever no reserved obligation carries the candidate's key, returning `this` only when one already does. So on every input that reaches it the comparison is false, and replacing it with false selects the same branch. The rule it states is real and enforced; the throw that states it is shadowed by the store check the loop makes first.

Reaching this disjunct means the first one was false, so the commit's kind is "invocation" or "eventDelivery". validateClosedShape gives each of those its own branch, and both demand a system writer: the invocation branch throws unless writer.kind is "system" with a receipt cause, the delivery branch unless it is "system" with a delivery cause. RunCommitCodec decodes through RunCommit.fromData and so through that constructor, and RunCommit has no other construction path, so a commit of either kind always carries a system writer and this test is constantly false. It is written because appendInTransaction and the evidence checks below read writer.cause, which the checker only allows once the union is narrowed. The mutants forcing the kind group the other way are killed by the merge and message commits the door now refuses.

The first disjunct has already established that the commit's kind is "message" or "verdict", and validateClosedShape routes both to its final block, which throws "Turn-authored commit fields are invalid" unless writer.kind is "turn". Since the codec decodes through RunCommit's constructor and nothing else constructs one, a message or verdict commit always has a turn writer, so this test never fires and removing it selects the same branch. The complementary mutant that forces the same test true — refusing every turn append — is killed, as are both halves of the kind group beside it, so the door's authority check remains asserted where it can actually decide.

By the time this disjunct is evaluated the commit's kind is "merge", and validateClosedShape's merge branch throws "Merge commit fields are invalid" unless the writer is a system writer with a control cause, along with two parents, a resolution, content and a receipt. Every RunCommit reaches that check on construction and the codec decodes through it, so a merge commit with any other writer cannot exist and this test is constantly false. The kind test beside it is what actually refuses commits at this door, and it is now asserted with a system-authored invocation — a commit carrying exactly the writer this disjunct looks for — so the two are told apart rather than shadowed.

Reaching this disjunct means the commit's kind is "undo", and validateClosedShape sends that kind through requireControl before anything else, which admits only a system writer with a control cause. The constructor runs that check on every RunCommit, including every one the codec decodes, so an undo commit with a turn or root writer is unconstructible and the test is constantly false. It is written so the door's refusal reads as one rule rather than two, and because the appendInTransaction path below distinguishes writer kinds; the kind half of the same condition is what does the refusing, and it is now exercised with a system-authored invocation.

Both operands of this disjunction are the same predicate about the same Run. The constructor sets lifecycle to active exactly when init.terminal is undefined, and stores the snapshot from that same field, so lifecycle.kind !== "terminal" holds precisely when terminal === undefined holds. For any predicate P, P || P and P && P have the same value, so flipping the operator between two spellings of one predicate cannot change the chain, and the clauses after it are evaluated on exactly the same inputs. This holds for every Run the package can produce, since Run.fromData constructs through the same constructor and no other path assigns either field.

Run derives its lifecycle from its terminal snapshot in the constructor — active when init.terminal is undefined and terminal otherwise — and assigns both from the same field of the same frozen init, which is the invariant the class comment states as "a Run is terminal exactly when it holds its terminal snapshot". So lifecycle.kind !== "terminal" and terminal === undefined are the same predicate, and the disjunct immediately after this one tests the second of them. Removing this one leaves that one to make the identical decision on every Run, including every Run the codec decodes, because Run.fromData builds through the same constructor. The mutant that forces this test true instead, refusing every captured append, is killed.

This disjunct is implied by the one before it for the same reason it implies it: Run's constructor sets lifecycle to terminal exactly when init.terminal is present, and stores both from one field, so a Run whose lifecycle is terminal always holds a snapshot. Where the first disjunct is false the second is false too, and where the first is true the chain has already short-circuited. What the test earns is not a refusal but a narrowing: the clause below it reads run.terminal.obligation.obligations, which the checker will not allow while the field is optional. Nothing observable changes when a redundant narrowing stops being evaluated.

Control reaches this disjunct only after the running-status test above it was false, so the Turn is running, and a running Turn holds a lease — Turn's constructor throws "Running Turns require a held lease" otherwise. TurnLease's constructor in turn throws "Held Turn leases require an expiration" for a held lease with no expiry, so expiresAt was read from a lease that has one and this test is constantly false. Even where the invariant not to hold, the mutant would go on to compute `undefined > now.getTime()`, which is NaN-false and selects the same branch. The test is written so the comparison below it typechecks against a number.

The optional call cannot short-circuit here. The branch is entered only when commit.kind is "migration", and validateClosedShape's migration branch throws "Migration commit fields are invalid" unless commit.migration is present — it also requires the commit's pins to equal the migration target. RunCommit's constructor runs that check on construction and RunCommitCodec decodes through it, so a migration commit always carries its migration record and both spellings read the same RunPins and call the same equals. The chain is written because the field's declared type stays optional for every commit kind, not because this site can meet an absent one.

Every commit that reaches this branch has exactly one parent. The branch is the else of `commit.kind === "merge"`, and validateClosedShape gives merge and root their own arities — two parents and none — while throwing "Unary Run commits require one parent" for every other kind. The only ways into appendInTransaction are the typed doors and the Turn transitions, which pass message, verdict, invocation, eventDelivery, undo, migration, checkpoint and result commits; the root commit is inserted at genesis through insertCommit and never appended. So the length test is constantly false, and the comparison beside it, which the parent-conflict tests do exercise, decides the branch on its own.

Turn's constructor pins holder to status: a queued Turn requires an unheld epoch-zero lease, a suspended or terminal Turn must be unheld, and a running Turn must hold one. So `status.kind === "running"` and `lease.holder !== undefined` are the same predicate over any constructed Turn, and the conjunct after this one already tests the second spelling. Forcing this one true leaves the same set of Turns selected by the undo fence check, on every Turn the repository can return, because TurnCodec decodes through that constructor. The mutant that forces it false instead, which would let undo run past an in-flight Turn, is killed.

This conjunct restates the one before it. A Turn holding a lease is a running Turn — the constructor refuses a queued Turn with any holder and refuses a suspended or terminal Turn with one — so wherever the running test has already passed, the holder is defined and this test is constantly true. Forcing it true therefore selects the same Turns for the undo fence, and the predicate keeps refusing exactly the in-flight Turns it refused before. It is written because the message it guards is about a held lease, and because the pair reads as the one fact SPEC §5.5 states; the mutant forcing it false is killed by the in-flight undo test.

Indexing an array with -1 yields undefined, which is the value the true arm of this conditional supplies, so the mutant computes the same `picked` on the one input the two spellings could differ on. The input is unreachable besides: validateClosedShape refuses a merge commit whose pick resolution does not name one of its own ordered parents, so indexOf over those parents' values always finds the resolution's parent and pickedIndex is 0 or 1 by the time this line runs. Neither arm has a side effect, and the two-element array literal is rebuilt identically either way.

This disjunct cannot fire. It is inside the pick-resolution branch, so the commit's kind is "merge", and validateClosedShape's merge branch throws "Merge commit fields are invalid" unless content is present — along with two parents, a system control writer, a resolution and a receipt. Every RunCommit passes that check on construction and the codec decodes through it, so commit.content is a ContentRef here and the test is constantly false. What it earns is the narrowing that lets `picked.content.equals(commit.content)` typecheck; the disjunct before it, about the picked parent's own content, is the one that can refuse and is killed.

The tree branch is entered only when commit.treeResolution is defined, and validateClosedShape refuses a merge commit whose tree resolution and tree checkpoint do not occur together — `(treeResolution === undefined) !== (treeCheckpoint === undefined)` throws "Tree resolution and checkpoint must occur together". So a commit with a resolution always carries a checkpoint, this test is constantly false, and the disjunct before it, about the selected parent's checkpoint, is what can refuse. The test is written so the equals call below it typechecks against a ContentRef rather than an optional one.

This flip makes the first three disjuncts a conjunction with the third, and the chain still refuses exactly what it refused. TurnInboxEntry's constructor forces the event and the cancellation token to agree, so the first and third operands are one fact and their conjunction equals either of them; and it forces the token to name the entry's own Turn, so an entry addressed elsewhere fails the leaseTokensEqual test that closes the chain. Every entry the original refused is still refused, with the same message, and every entry it admitted still passes each operand. All four operands are pure reads and comparisons.

TurnInboxEntry's constructor ties the event to the token: it throws "Only turn.cancel entries carry an exact cancellation token" whenever `(event === "turn.cancel") !== (cancellationToken !== undefined)`, so being a cancel entry and carrying a token are one fact, and the codec decodes through that constructor. This disjunct therefore holds exactly when the cancellationToken disjunct two lines below holds, and removing it leaves that one to raise the same refusal with the same message. The clause between them is a pure comparison of two TurnIds, so evaluating it where the original short-circuited changes nothing.

The two disjuncts this span covers are both implied by what follows. The event test holds exactly when the cancellation-token test one line below holds, because TurnInboxEntry's constructor refuses an entry whose event and token disagree. The Turn test is implied by the token comparison at the end of the chain: the same constructor requires cancellationToken.turn to equal the entry's own turn, and the displaced token names the Turn being cancelled, so an entry addressed to another Turn cannot carry a token equal to it. Forcing the pair false therefore leaves the later disjuncts to raise the same refusal on exactly the same entries.

This disjunct is the other half of the same constructor invariant that makes the event test redundant: TurnInboxEntry refuses an entry whose event and cancellation token disagree, so an entry with no token is not a turn.cancel entry and has already been caught by the event test at the top of the chain. It is written here for the narrowing that leaseTokensEqual needs, since the field's declared type is optional. Where it would be the first true disjunct the chain has already thrown, and where the entry does carry a token it is false, so no input can separate the two.

A terminal Turn never holds a lease. Turn's constructor throws "Suspended and terminal Turns must be unheld" for exactly the combination this disjunct looks for, using the same isTerminal predicate the operand before it uses, and TurnCodec decodes through that constructor, so the filter's second test can never be the one that selects a sibling. Forcing it false leaves `!isTerminalTurn(sibling)` choosing the same pending set, and the forced-cancellation evidence the terminalization then demands is unchanged. The test is written because the pending set is about siblings that are still live in either sense.

The conjunct guards the else arm, where left is known to be present, so forcing it true leaves `left.equals(right)`. The two differ only when right is undefined, and there the call answers false rather than throwing: the single call site passes ContentRefs, ContentRef extends TextId, and TextId.equals begins with `typeof other === "object"`, which is false for undefined, so it returns before reading a private field. The original's short circuit and the mutant's call therefore both yield false. The helper is a pure comparison of two frozen references and its result feeds a boolean chain, so nothing else can carry a difference.

A result commit always carries content. The conjunct before this one is isTurnAuthored("result", token), which returns false unless the commit's kind is "result", and validateClosedShape routes that kind to its final block, which throws "Turn-authored commit fields are invalid" unless content is present. RunCommitCodec decodes through RunCommit's constructor, so every commit listCommits yields has passed that check, and this test is constantly true wherever it is evaluated. It is written so the comparison after it has a ContentRef to hand rather than an optional one; that comparison, against the Turn's own recorded result, is killed by the unpaired result commit test.

The optional call cannot short-circuit. The disjunct before it is `!commit.isTurnAuthored("checkpoint", this.token)`, and isTurnAuthored returns true only when the commit's kind is "checkpoint", which validateClosedShape admits only with a turn writer, a subject Turn and content present. So reaching this expression means content is a ContentRef, and both spellings call the same ContentRef.equals against the checkpoint's state. The chain is written because RunCommit types content as optional for every kind; a test could only separate the two by producing a checkpoint commit without content, which the record's own constructor refuses.

Turn's constructor makes holding a lease and running the same fact: it refuses a queued Turn with any holder, refuses a suspended or terminal Turn with one, and refuses a running Turn without one. So wherever the conjunct before this one has already established that the status is running, the holder is defined and this test is constantly true. Forcing it true leaves the token comparison that follows deciding whether the recovered cancellation belongs to the lease this call still holds, on exactly the Turns it decided before, for every Turn TurnCodec can decode.

This conjunct is the same fact as the one after it. A Turn that holds a lease is running — Turn's constructor refuses a holder on a queued, suspended or terminal Turn — so forcing the status test true cannot admit a Turn the holder test does not also admit. Recovery therefore treats exactly the same Turns as holding the current lease, and the §5.6 rule it implements, that a cancellation delivered against a live lease is the holder's to settle, keeps applying to the same set. The mutant that flips the operator between the two, which does change the grouping of the chain, is killed.

A commit with a turn writer always names a subject Turn. The method returns false immediately unless writer.kind is "turn", and validateClosedShape admits a turn writer only from its final block, the one reached by message, checkpoint, result and verdict commits, which throws unless subjectTurn is present — every other kind is routed to a branch demanding a root or system writer. RunCommit's constructor runs that check and the codec decodes through it, so the optional call never short-circuits and both spellings compare the same TurnId. The chain is written because subjectTurn is optional across the union of kinds.

Forcing this conjunct true leaves `left.equals(right)` for the case where left is a TurnId and right is undefined, and TurnId inherits TextId.equals, which tests `typeof other === "object"` first and so answers false for undefined instead of throwing. That is the same false the short circuit produced. Both call sites pass a commit's subjectTurn against the subject Turn of the evidence backing it, so the operands are frozen ids and the result feeds a refusal chain; no input can make the two spellings disagree, and the helper has no other effect.

Number.isSafeInteger, tested immediately after this disjunct, coerces nothing and returns false for every argument that is not a number, so a string, boolean, null, array or object value is rejected by it whether or not the typeof test ran first. The mutant therefore computes the same boolean on every input and raises the same TypeError with the same subject. The typeof test earns its place in the type system, where it narrows JsonValue | undefined to number so that `value < 0` and the number return typecheck — the standard library declares isSafeInteger as returning boolean rather than as a type predicate, so it cannot narrow on its own.

Flipping this operator turns two disjuncts into a conjunction, and both are implied by disjuncts later in the same chain, so the chain's value is unchanged. TurnInboxEntry's constructor makes carrying a cancellation token and being a turn.cancel entry one fact, so where the event test was the true one the token test below still fires; and it requires the token to name the entry's own Turn, so where the Turn test was the true one the leaseTokensEqual test below still fires against a token naming a different Turn. Every operand is a pure comparison, so evaluating more of them changes nothing but the order.
